entry.title: How Indiana artists and Purdue Engineers made the Neil Armstrong Space Prize

media:group.media:title: How Indiana artists and Purdue Engineers made the Neil Armstrong Space Prize
media:group.media:description:
How was the Neil Armstrong Space Prize made? Purdue University's newest and most prestigious space honor began as a hand-sculpted clay relief. It was then 3D scanned and CNC machined from titanium, all on Purdue's West Lafayette campus.
Hoosier sculptor Bill Wolfe and designer Wade Biggs of Deer Ridge Woodcraft developed the design together. It has Neil Armstrong's portrait on the front and the Apollo 11 bootprint on the back. Biggs describes working through as many as 100 to 200 thumbnails to land on a design worthy of a global award.
The clay original was digitized using the ZEISS ScanBox in the Build@Scale Lab. Each image the scanner captures can record up to 12 million points, so the scan preserves every detail of the sculptor's work. Paul McPherson, director of the Bechtel Innovation Design Center, and graduate student Kylea Hughes refined that data into a usable model. Anirudh Pal then tested whether it could be manufactured, chose the tooling and fixtures, and set up CAM programming for the center's CNC mills. Each titanium medallion takes about 25 hours of machine time.
The first medallions went to the inaugural laureates, SpaceX's Falcon 9 Booster Landing Team. The project shows what's possible when artists, engineers and students work toward the same goal: honoring a Purdue alum whose first step reshaped humanity's view of what's possible, and inspiring whoever takes the next one.

entry.title: Neil Armstrong Space Prize 2026: Full Award Ceremony

media:group.media:title: Neil Armstrong Space Prize 2026: Full Award Ceremony
media:group.media:description:
Watch the full ceremony for the inaugural Neil Armstrong Space Prize. Purdue University awarded it to SpaceX's Falcon 9 Booster Landing Team for making reusable rockets part of everyday spaceflight.
What is the Neil Armstrong Space Prize? It is Purdue's new international honor for the achievements in space exploration with the most consequential impact on humanity. It is awarded in the categories of Discovery, Innovation and Human Achievement. The first prize recognizes a team that took booster landing from a bold experiment to routine operations: more than 600 Falcon 9 missions have flown, with lower launch costs and a faster launch cadence.
The evening includes remarks from Purdue President Mitch Daniels and a keynote from NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who noted that Neil Armstrong carried the work of an extraordinary team down the ladder with him. Purdue astronaut Jerry Ross introduces the selection committee. Mark Lundstrom, the John A. Edwardson Dean of the College of Engineering, joins in presenting medals to Lars Blackmore, Shana Diez, Jonathan Edwards, Yoshiaki Kuwata and Eduardo Velazquez. Each recipient shares what it took to get there: years of persistence, failures along the way and hundreds of teammates behind every landing. Members of the Armstrong family and Purdue's Cradle of Astronauts attend the ceremony.
Read the full story: https://bit.ly/4dEf1mK
Watch the full video featured in the event: https://bit.ly/4h6eF9A

entry.title: Purdue AI Racing sets track record during Indy Autonomous Challenge at Laguna Seca

media:group.media:title: Purdue AI Racing sets track record during Indy Autonomous Challenge at Laguna Seca
media:group.media:description:
Purdue AI Racing (PAIR) set a new track record at WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca and finished runner-up in the Indy Autonomous Challenge's first-ever autonomous overtaking competition on a road course. Go behind the scenes with the team before, during and after race day at the Mission Grand Prix of Monterey.
This video follows PAIR, the only American university competing among this year's top teams, as they prepare for a course that's demanding even for professional human drivers. Team members and faculty advisors explain how a year of data from Laguna Seca helped refine the car's control algorithms and perception and tracking logic, and how the team adapted its strategy for an overtaking competition format that's new to this track. What does an autonomous overtaking competition actually look like? The video breaks it down: the lead car defends its line while the trailing car works to pass, with the two swapping roles and the pace escalating until one side can't keep up.
The result: a record-setting time trial lap and a hard-fought run in the overtaking competition.
